summary: Contains a revised specification of the Internet Stream Protocol version 2, a protocol for carrying real-time streams with resource reservation. It is experimental and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: ST2+ is an experimental protocol for setting up one-way streams to one or more receivers with requested quality-of-service properties. It reserves resources before sending data, but does not guarantee recovery from lost data packets.

questions: what is scmp stream control message protocol
subtitle: An experimental protocol for setting up resource-reserved streams for real-time traffic.

tldr.problem: Real-time applications may need bounded delay and reserved network resources that best-effort IP does not promise.
tldr.mechanism: ST2+ uses SCMP to establish a one-way stream and negotiate a flow specification, then uses a compact ST header to forward data along accepted paths.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1819 is Historic and was published as Experimental. It obsoletes RFC 1190; the IESG note says neither version is an Internet Standard.

today: RFC 1819 is Historic and was published as an Experimental specification. It obsoletes RFC 1190, and its IESG note says neither version is an Internet Standard or under consideration for that status.

sections.title: What ST2+ Is Designed to Do
sections.content:
Internet Stream Protocol version 2 (ST2) is an experimental connection-oriented protocol at the same layer as IP. It was designed for applications such as real-time audio, video, and distributed simulation that request a quality of service (QoS) from the network. ST2 is an adjunct to IP, not a replacement for it.

ST2+ separates data transfer, called ST, from stream setup and control, called the Stream Control Message Protocol (SCMP). Before data transfer, the network selects paths to targets and asks local resource managers to reserve resources. The IESG note says neither this version nor the previous version is an Internet Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: ST2+ is designed to reserve network resources for real-time data before sending it. It works alongside IP and was published as an experimental protocol, not an Internet Standard.

sections.title: Streams and Resource Reservation
sections.content:
A stream is a one-way path from an origin to one or more targets, arranged as a routing tree. ST agents at hosts and routers maintain stream state. The RFC defines the ST data protocol, SCMP setup protocol, and ST2+ flow specification, while assuming a routing function and Local Resource Manager (LRM) at each node.

During setup, SCMP presents the flow specification to each LRM. The LRM checks whether resources are available, calculates achievable QoS, reserves resources, and later schedules access to enforce the negotiated service. The routing and LRM interfaces are local matters and are not specified by this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A stream connects one sender to one or more receivers through a route chosen for the stream. Each node checks and reserves its own resources before accepting the path.

sections.title: ST Data Packets
sections.content:
An ST packet has a 12-byte header. It includes an ST version, a bit distinguishing data from control, a packet-drop priority, the packet length, a header checksum, and a Stream Identifier made from a unique identifier and the stream origin's IPv4 address. The ST identifier lets an agent find the stream's forwarding information.

ST data transfer is unreliable: ST does not recover lost packets and does not checksum the data. An application must segment data to fit the minimum MTU along the stream because ST does not fragment packets. During congestion, agents attempt to discard lower-priority packets first.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet carries a stream identifier so routers can forward it along the established path. ST does not retransmit lost data, so applications must choose packet sizes that fit the path.

sections.title: Setting Up and Changing a Stream
sections.content:
SCMP uses requests and responses, with retransmission after a timeout to handle missing control messages. To establish a stream, the origin chooses an identifier, selects next hops through its routing function, asks its LRM to reserve resources, and sends CONNECT messages toward the targets. Intermediate agents repeat the process along their paths.

Targets accept or refuse the request, and the result travels back toward the origin. The origin can later add or remove targets, request a QoS change, or close the stream. Targets may also request to join when the stream's join authorization permits it. Agents use periodic HELLO messages to detect neighbor failures.
sections.plainLanguage: The origin sends a setup request through each node on the route. Each node checks resources, and the target's acceptance returns to the origin before the path is ready for data.

sections.title: The Flow Specification
sections.content:
The ST2+ FlowSpec describes a QoS class, precedence, message size, message rate, and end-to-end delay. For the size, rate, and delay values, the application supplies a desired value and an acceptable limit. Each LRM updates the actual value along the path; if it cannot meet the limit, setup on that path fails.

The required predictive class allows negotiated QoS to be violated briefly and reserves for normal conditions. The optional guaranteed class reserves for the worst case and does not permit QoS violations, which may require more resources. The RFC states that the range between minimum and maximum delay bounds delay jitter.
sections.plainLanguage: The application states its preferred service level and the worst level it can accept. Each node reports what it can actually provide, and the path is rejected if that falls below the limit.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's Security Considerations section says that security issues are not discussed in the memo. It does not define a security mechanism for ST2+.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not analyze security or specify security protections for ST2+.
